opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the way to understand it is to start from biology. If you look at how animals, and humans, walk over rough terrain, vision plays a very particular role. It's not that you're looking at your feet at every step. In fact, studies of human walking show that we look a couple of steps ahead. The visual system is planning: where am I going to put my foot, is there a step coming up, is that a patch of loose gravel or a slippery surface? By the time your foot actually lands, your eyes have already moved on, and what's taking care of that step is a combination of memory of what you saw and proprioception, your body's sense of its own joints and forces.

So in our work on legged robots, we came at it in stages. First we asked how far you can get with no vision at all, a "blind" robot that relies purely on proprioception. And you can get surprisingly far. With learned policies trained in simulation, with a lot of variation in terrain, mass, and friction, and with the ability to adapt online to what the legs are feeling, a quadruped can walk on grass, sand, rubble, even stairs to some degree. It's reacting, feeling its way.

But there are clear limits to being blind. If there's a big step or a gap, you discover it by bumping into it or falling into it. That's where vision comes in: it lets you anticipate. You see the stair before you reach it, and you adjust your gait so you lift your leg high enough at the right moment. The interesting technical point is that the camera sees the terrain in front of the robot, but by the time the robot's legs get there, that terrain is underneath the body and out of view. So the policy has to carry a kind of short-term memory, integrating what it saw a moment ago with what the legs are feeling now. That's very much analogous to what humans do.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that we don't have to hand-engineer a terrain map, build a precise 3D reconstruction, and then do classical planning over it. You can learn an end-to-end, or nearly end-to-end, policy that goes from depth or image input plus proprioception straight to motor commands, trained largely in simulation and transferred to the real world. Vision then isn't a separate module that produces a geometric model for some downstream planner; it's in service of action. That reflects a broader view I hold: perception and action shouldn't be studied in isolation. Vision evolved to guide movement, and if we want robots that move with the agility of animals, we should build their visual systems in that spirit.

r001.rationale: The response says a blind quadruped can walk surprisingly far on several terrains, but does not state that it can walk without vision most of the time.

r002.rationale: It explains that vision anticipates steps and gaps and helps the robot place and lift its feet at the right time on difficult terrain.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the right way to think about it is in terms of the biology. If you look at how animals, and humans, walk over rough ground, vision is not doing everything. There's a very important role for proprioception, for touch, for the sense of where your limbs are and what forces you're feeling through your feet. If I close my eyes and you put me on a rocky trail, I can still make progress, because my body is responding to what it feels. I'll be slow and a bit clumsy, but I won't fall over immediately.

So in our work on legged robots, that was actually the first thing we did. We trained policies that walk using only proprioception, no cameras at all, and they turn out to be remarkably robust. The robot learns to adapt, in a fraction of a second, to the fact that it stepped on something soft, or slippery, or that there's a step it didn't expect. That's the reactive layer, and it's essential.

But vision gives you something proprioception can't, which is anticipation. If there's a gap in front of you, or a set of stairs, or a boulder, you don't want to find out about it by stepping into it. You want to see it from a couple of meters away and start planning your foot placement in advance. Humans do this very naturally. If you watch people hiking, their gaze is fixating on the spots where they're going to put their feet a step or two ahead. There's beautiful work in the psychology literature on this.

So the way I understand it, vision in locomotion is really about terrain geometry a few steps ahead, and about coupling that to the body. And the interesting technical problem is how to combine the two. You have this fast feedback loop from the legs, and you have a slower, more predictive signal from the camera, and the policy has to learn to trust each one appropriately. We've found that if you train with the right kind of simulation, with lots of varied terrain, and you let the robot learn end to end from the depth images to the joint commands, it can do things like walk up stairs, step over gaps, traverse stepping stones, that are simply impossible with the blind policy.

And I'd say the lesson generalizes beyond locomotion. Vision isn't an abstract perception module that hands a nice 3D map to a planner. In the animal, and I think in a good robot, it's deeply tied to action. You see in order to move, and what you need to see is determined by what you're about to do.

r001.rationale: The response says legged robots can walk robustly using only proprioception, but it does not state that a robot dog can do so most of the time.

r002.rationale: It explains that vision helps anticipate gaps, stairs, and boulders so the robot can plan precise foot placement ahead of time.

astra-6.text:
I think vision gives a robot the ability to anticipate. If you’re walking over rocky ground, you don’t wait until your foot hits a rock to discover that it’s there. You look ahead and use that information to decide where to place your feet, how high to lift them, and perhaps whether to take a different route.

But vision alone isn’t enough. You can see a patch of ground, yet you may not know whether it’s slippery or whether it will give way under your weight. So the robot has to combine what it sees with what it feels through contact and with information about its own body. Vision helps plan the movement; feedback lets you adjust as you execute it. The interesting challenge is making those work together.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that the robot dog can walk without vision most of the time.

r002.rationale: It explains that vision helps a robot anticipate rocky terrain and decide where to place its feet, making foot placement a reason vision matters for locomotion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision gives the robot the ability to anticipate. If you’re walking over rocky ground, you don’t wait until your foot hits a rock to decide what to do. You look ahead, identify possible footholds, and adjust your steps. A robot needs that same connection between seeing and acting.

But vision alone isn’t enough. An image can suggest that a surface is flat, but it may not tell you whether it’s slippery or whether it will support your weight. So the robot has to combine what it sees with feedback from contact and from its own motion. Vision helps it plan where to go; that feedback helps it adapt as it goes.

r001.rationale: The response does not say the robot dog can walk without vision most of the time.

r002.rationale: It explains that on rocky ground the robot uses vision to identify footholds and adjust its steps, describing why vision matters for foot placement during locomotion.
